text:

IMPORTANT: Create a GitHub account
IMPORTANT Post your GitHub username on the GitHub Usernames google sheet. After roughly 10 minutes (during normal working hours), you should receive two emails. One email will be an invitation from “GitHub” to join the BYUI335 organization. Accept the invitation. The other email will be an invitation from “Katie Allen” to collaborate on a repository with your name on it. Accept the invitation. If you do not see the two emails, check your spam folder.

Normally you would create your own repository, but because we want your class repository saved in a special organization we are creating it for you. You will be using this repository to turn in assignments.

Join the Data Science Society workspace in Slack. This is where we will have class conversations and ask questions. Here is the link to join: https://join.slack.com/t/byuidss/signup . The following sub-bullets provide additional detailed instructions about setting up and using slack.

Create a professional username, something you could share with an employer
In addition to the channels you are automatically add to, be sure to join the following two channels:

Our class channel. It will look something like #ds350_s22_allen or #ds350_s22_woodruff. Find the appropriate channel and add yourself to it. Once you are in the class channel, introduce yourself by replying to the introduction thread by clicking the thread, hit reply, then type a brief introduction.
#tutoring_lab, add this channel. It is where you can ask questions about code related to specific tasks or case studies.
Browse through the channels and join as as many as you are interested in. This community will be a great resource, even if you are not a Data Science major.

Extra features are available when you install Slack as an app on your PC and/or phone. The more comfortable you become with using Slack, the easier it will be to collaborate with each other throughout your professional career.

Post a professional picture to your GitHub, LinkedIn, and Slack icons. Go to the BYU-Idaho LinkedIn Photobooth if you don’t have a professional picture.
Make plans to attend Data Science Society on the second Wednesday of the semester.
Download the R script first-R-script.R and open it in RStudio. Run each line of code, one at a time (figure out the keyboard shortcut to do this). Note any questions you want to ask your group when you get to class.

It is not crucial that you understand what each line of code does at this point in the semester. However, briefly try guessing what each line of code does before running it, but don’t worry if you don’t understand all (or any of) the code.




Git is a program that helps you organize code and keep track of any changes you make. Git uses folders called “repositories” to organize code into different projects. GitHub is an online platform where you can store your Git repositories, and then access them from any computer. You will use Git and GitHub this semester to submit your homework, in a repository made specifically for this class.

Study Chapter 8: R for Data Science—Projects
Install Git on your computer. Then link the repository we created for you on GitHub to an RStudio project dedicated specifically to this class. Either read these instructions or watch this video that walks you through the process of setting everything up and ensuring RStudio is talking to GitHub. If you can’t get it to work, reach out for help! This is a critical step to being able to turn in assignments.






Warning



If you didn’t put your Github info on the google sheet referenced in the “pre” part of this task, and accept the two invitations, then you will need to do so ASAP. Do not simply create your own repository since we want the repository to belong to our class organization.


After completing step 2 above , edit the README.md in RStudio to include a short description of yourself, and “push” the changes to the online version of your repository.
To practice “pulling”:

Now edit your README.md file from online instead of from within RStudio. Navigate to your repository and open the readme.md file. Below your description, add links to the repos of everyone in your group (you may need to finish this part in class, or ask them over slack).
Go back to RStudio. Notice that the repo links do not appear in your README.md
Using the terminal (next to the console) or Git tab in RStudio, pull the online changes you made to update the files on your hard drive.
Let’s make one more change to README.md in RStudio by adding the name of your group. Then push the change to GitHub online.


You will want to get in the habit of pull, add/stage, commit, push (in that order!) at least once everyday.


Once you have completed all that you can for the week, include a link to the readme.md file in the Week 1 Submission on I-learn. Don’t submit multiple times to the submission box in I-learn, just submit 1 time at the end of the week and include all the links to what you want graded that week.

title: 2  First Rmd
text:
ReadingPrePost



Making your first R Markdown File
Chapter 27: R for Data Science—R Markdown
Chapter 30: R for Data Science—R Markdown workflow
R Markdown cheat sheet (a summary of the highlights from the reading for future, quick reference)




Install the DS350 RMarkdown template. This template automatically keeps the .md file and formats the report the way we like. You MUST use this template for all future markdown files.

An ‘.md’ is essentially a text file and it renders nicely in GitHub so we can easily see each other’s work there. (The .Rmd file is a text file with code chunks and doesn’t render well on GitHub, nor does the .html files)

Create an .Rmd file in RStudio using the RMD Template for this class, after making te following changes try knitting it.

Title it “Task 2pre”
Just to give you practice putting code in a file, add the R code below to your .Rmd file in an R chunk:


plot(x = iris$Sepal.Length,  
     y = iris$Petal.Length, 
     col = iris$Species, 
     pch = 19)
Try to get help if things don’t go smoothly. Ask questions in slack or at the lab. If issues persist, note any questions, errors, or problems you have and plan to ask them in class (i.e. this is considered “successfully stuck”).



Find three or four articles that use data and visualizations to answer a question

Use any website, blog, or article with good visualizations.
Some fun websites to try are The Pudding, FiveThirtyEight, Our World in Data, and Priceonomics.

While in the R project for this class’ repository, start a new .Fmd file using the DS350 Rmd template. Remove what’s there by default. Put a link to each article in the .Rmd file. Also, write a one-paragraph review of each article that answers the following questions:

What is unique or good about the visualization? List a few ideas.
What could be better? Identify at least one issue with the visualization.




Knit the file to .html and keep the .md file as well (this will happen automatically if you used the template). Push your .md, .html, and .Rmd files to your Github repository.
NOTE: As was mentioned above, the DS350 template automatically keeps the MD file and formats the page the way we like. For instructions on getting and using the template read here, same link as step 1 above You MUST use this template for all future markdown files.

title: 4  Few Layers, Many Rows
text:
ResourcesBackgroundPrePost





Chapter 3.1-3.6: R for Data Science—Visualization
Chapter 7: R for Data Science—Exploratory Data Analysis
Plotting large datasets




Guided instruction materials are tailored to this course and often have extra hints/emphasis to help you complete the task. These exercises assume you have read the material. They provide you an opportunity to practice while providing additional explanation. Solutions for the exercises are provided at the bottom of the file. You can think of this like a chance to “look in the back of the book.” These activities are not graded or turned in. You can use them however you like, to your best benefit.

Read and complete the exercises in the .Rmd file (you may wish to knit the file first for easier reading): ggplotting with many layers




You just started your internship at a big firm in New York, and your manager gave you an extensive file of flights that departed JFK, LGA, or EWR in 2013. From this data (which you can obtain in R) your manager wants you draw some insights.
Before we can start to answer business questions we need to become familiar with our data. If one is provided, you may want to start with the data dictionary. However, you can also just dive into the data and gain an understanding based on the variable names and types.
We will also want to know how the variables relate to each other. We can create tables or visualizations that summarize how different variables relate to each other. At this point, we are deepening our understanding as well as beginning our analysis.



Create a new .Rmd to do this task. Don’t forget to load (not install) the tidyverse package.
Use the nycflights13::flights dataset. (You may need to install nycflights13 package first).

Note the use of double colon allows you to access functions and datasets from a package without loading the entire package.
You can run ?nycflights13::flights in the console to learn more about the variables in the dataset. (Don’t include this in your Rmarkdown).

Pick two variables (columns) whose relationship you would like to explore.

Provide a visualization of the univariate distribution of each of the selected variables separately (i.e. 2 plots are needed here, 1 for each variable)
Build bivariate summaries of the variables you have chosen to investigate (1 plot is needed here, the plot should contain both variables in it).

Write one to two paragraphs in the .Rmd summarizing insights from your graphics and your data presentation choices.
Knit your .Rmd and then push your .Rmd, .md, .html into your git repository.



Make at least two significant improvements to what you created as part of the pre class tasks and push to GitHub.


In I-learn submit a link to the .md file on GitHub.

title: 6  Great British Bake Off
text:
ResourcesBackgroundPrePost




Chapter 10: Tibbles




data structures
The previous guided instruction could still be helpful if you have not yet completed it: data wrangling with dplyr




The Great British Bake Off was a hit reality TV show that put amateur bakers against each other. Contestants were eliminated in each round until a winner was crowned. The show ran for 12 seasons (a season is called a series in the dataset) through 2021, with plenty of drama. You will analyze the show’s 7-day viewership (i.e. TV ratings over a 7 day period).
Specifically, you want to know how the 7-day viewership changes within a season and across seasons. In one graph, you compare the 7-day viewership for the season’s premiere and finale. In another graph, you compare the mean across seasons while not losing track of each episode’s 7-day viewership.



Read in the TV ratings data for the show using the following code. We will be using the ratings dataset. You can learn more about the data set by running ?ratings.
install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("apreshill/bakeoff")
library(bakeoff)
Create a chart to illustrate the differences in seven-day viewership between the first and last episode of each season respectively.
Write a paragraph in your .Rmd file to discuss the historical trends and the way the finale viewership behaves.
We are curious how the mean ratings have changed across seasons (aka series) for the Great British Bake Off. We also want to see how ratings progress for each episode within a season. More specifically, for seasons with 10 episodes, sketch a chart that displays the 7 day ratings for each episode per season (aka series) and how mean ratings change across seasons.

In your sketch, be sure to fully think through and label the axes and other aspects of the chart.
Now make a sketch on paper of what the underlying dataset for that chart should look like (i.e. what are the column, what do the rows contain, etc.)

Bring your 2 sketches (one of the chart, and one of the dataset) to class. Also be sure your .md file containing the answers to points 2 and 3 above is on GitHub so that you can easily share it with classmates.




Again, start with the ratings dataset. Create the graph you sketched (or an improved version) as part of the pre class work for this task.

Use/add on to the file you started in the pre class tasks.
Remember, this chart should only include seasons with 10 episodes.

Write at least one paragraph discussing your visualization. Point out interesting insights you see in the plot. Perhaps a little internet surfing or Googling will help you find reasons for the viewership changes.



Push all your files to GitHub. In I-learn paste the link to the .md file that contains all your work for the pre and post tasks on GitHub: 2 charts and 2 paragraphs of writing (one about each chart).

title: 8  Wings to Fly
text:

You just started your internship at a big firm in New York, and your manager gave you an extensive file of flights that departed JFK, LGA, or EWR in 2013. From this data (which you can obtain in R) your manager wants you to answer some specific questions. :

For each origin airport (JFK, EWR, LGA), which airline has the lowest 75th percentile of delay time for flights scheduled to leave earlier than noon?
Which origin airport is best to minimize my chances of a late arrival when I am using Delta Airlines?
Which destination airport is the worst airport for arrival delays? You decide on the metric for “worst.”

title: 9  Clean and Reformat (aka Tidy) Stock Data
text:
ResourcesBackgroundPrePost





Chapter 11.5: R for Data Science—Writing and Saving Data
Chapter 12: R for Data Science—Tidy Data
RDS vs. RData

By the way, contrary to what the article suggests, I don’t believe saving your workspace is a good idea unless you think you’ll need it. It just slows down your computer. That’s the point of a script or markdown file, all the code is already saved so you can reproduce the workspace if necessary.

Raw vs. blob

Read this for a short written explanation of getting the right url from GitHub
This video shows examples of using the correct url to read in the data.






tidyr
Reading and Writing R files




In 1973 Princeton University professor Burton Malkiel said

In 1990 the Wall Street Journal took Burton up on his challenge. They ran this challenge until 2002 and pitted random dart throwing selections to expert picks.

We have access to stock return data through 1998. Open the dataset and get familiar with it. The “PROS” rows contain returns that professional investors were able to achieve at that date. The “DARTS” rows contain returns of stocks that were selected by monkeys randomly throwing darts. The “DJIA” rows contain returns for stocks in the Dow Jones Industrial Average. The Dow Jones Industrial Average is a group of 30 stocks for large companies with stable earnings. This “index” of stocks is one of the oldest, most closely watched indices in the world and is designed to serve as a proxy, or indicator, of the United States economy in general. (learn about about “the Dow”.)
We want to look at the returns for each six-month period of the year in which the returns were reported.



Use the appropriate function in library(readr) to read in the .RDS file found on GitHub

Depending on your computer, you should use read_rds(url("WEBLOCATION.RDS")) or read_rds("WEBLOCATION.RDS") to download and read the .RDS file type. Remember, R is case sensitive.
When using file paths to read files in from Github (and other locations), you must pay attention to ‘raw’ vs. ‘blob’ (seeing the reading below).

The contestant_period column is not “tidy” we want to create a month_end and a year_end column from the information it contains.
Save your “tidy” data as an .rds object.
Create a plot that shows the six-month returns by the year in which the returns are collected. Your plot should highlight the tighter spread of the DJIA as compared to the other two selection methods, DARTS and PROS.
Include your plot in an .Rmd file with a short paragraph describing your plots. Play with code-folding to make sure your code is displayed in your file (though have it default to hidden).

title: 10  Mean Heights of Countries Over Time
text:
ResourcesBackgroundPrePost





Chapter 18: R for Data Science—Pipes
Chapter 20: R for Data Science—Vectors
ALL of Chapter 11: R for Data Science—Data Import
readxl R package
downloader R package

BONUS: rio is the name of an R package that simplifies the reading in process. Instead of worrying about matching data types with the necessary package, you can just use import() from the rio package and it will figure it out for you. It can also read in a zipped file. (*Note: for zipped folders you can experiment with rio::import_list or the archive package.)



Data structures and importing data



The Scientific American argues that humans have been getting taller over the years. As the data scientists that we are becoming, we would like to find data that validates this concept.
This project is not as severe as the two quotes below, but it will give you a taste of pulling various data and file formats together into “tidy” data for visualization and analysis.

“Classroom data are like teddy bears and real data are like a grizzly bear with salmon blood dripping out its mouth.” Jenny Bryan


“Up to 80% of data analysis is spent on the process of cleaning and preparing data” Hadley Wickham




Read in and tidy the Worldwide heights estimates .xlsx file

Make sure the file is in long format with year as a column. See Example of the Tidy Excel File after formatting
Use the separate() and mutate() functions to create a decade column.

To check your work and verify there are no data issues, make a plot with decade on the x-axis and and all the countries heights in inches on the y-axis; with the points from Germany highlighted based on the data from the .xlsx file.

Don’t worry about formatting and labelling the plot too much at this point. You will do that as part of the post class task.

Knit the .Rmd file. Push your .Rmd, .md, and .html files into your GitHub repository.




Fix whatever issues you discovered in your data/plot by sharing with others in class.
Improve the visualization. Take time to fine tune the formatting and labelling.
Write a paragraph to summarize how you would respond to the assertion that humans are getting taller over the years. (Does your data tell a story?)

title: 11  Combining Height Files
text:
ResourcesBackgroundPrePost




Scan the reading to learn what types of files these packages are used to read in.

Haven package
foreign R package and read.dbf()

Be sure to do the Readings and Guided Instruction for the previous task if you have not yet.



The Scientific American argues that humans have been getting taller over the years. As the data scientists that we are becoming, we would like to find data that validates or refutes this concept. Our challenge is to show different male heights across the centuries.
This time, instead of looking at the mean height per country over time like we did for the previous task, we have a few files that contain heights of individuals. Each file represents a different time and/or place from which the individuals are sampled. We will combine the data from these files into one dataset to facilitate our visualization.



Work with these datasets where each row represents an individual. Import these five datasets into R and combine them into one tidy dataset.

German male conscripts in Bavaria, 19th century: Stata format.
Heights of bavarian male conscripts, 19th century: Stata format.
Heights of south-east and south-west german soldiers born in the 18th century: DBF format.

This file is zipped. After downloading it with download(), trying using unzip() and read.dbf() to load the data into R.
Can you tell which column is the birth year? HINT: Google translate may be helpful.

Bureau of Labor Statistics Height Data: csv format

Note: There is no birth year, so just assume mid-20th century and use 1950 as birth year

University of Wisconsin National Survey Data: SPSS (.sav) format

You’ll want to look here to understand this dataset and know which columns to use: National Survey Codebook


After your wrangling, each dataset should only contain the following columns:

We want to examine how heights have changed over time. Three of the data sets consist of just men, while 2 have both men and women. Filter to just focus on men.
Wrangle each dataset so that it contains the following columns: birth_year, height.in, height.cm, and study. You will have to do some conversions between inches and centimeters. You need to create the “study” column yourself to identify which dataset the rows came from.
For each dataset select(birth_year, height.in, height.cm, study)

Use the bind_rows() function to combine your five individual datasets into one dataset.
Write a short paragraph summarizing the data wrangling process you had to go through to create your tidy dataset. Include in that discussion any decisions you had to make about what data to exclude.

You may want to run some simple summary statistics or visuals to aid in the comparison of your dataset with the dataset of your group members.

Knit the .Rmd file. Push your .Rmd, .md, and .html files into your GitHub repository.

Make a small-multiples plot (i.e. facets) of the five studies containing individual heights to examine the question of height distribution across centuries.



Make two graphs to examine the question of height distribution across centuries.

One graph should show individual heights (not summaries) and be faceted by study.
The other graph is a graph of your choice that tries to answer the question. For example, you could try creating a “decade” column and showing height summaries by decade.

Write at least two paragraphs to address the following:

How would you respond to the assertion that humans are getting taller over time based on the datasets in this task’s analysis?
How does the story told by this data compare to the story told by the data in the previous task? Do they agree or do they contradict? If they contradict, reason through the contradiction and try to make sense of it.
Be sure to provide an overall conclusion about where you stand on the question.

title: 15  Data Search
text:
ReadingsBackgroundPrePost


Finding data to answer your question


Finding good data takes time, and can take longer than the time to tidy your data. This task could easily take three to six hours to find the data you need for your semester project. You may not finish this task this week, but you should definitely start it so that you are not rushed at the end of the semester. After you find good, potential data sources pick one to focus on working with for this task.


Create an .rmd file that has links to data sources with a description of the quality of each.
- Find 3-5 potential data sources (that are free) and document some information about the source. Choose one dataset to focus on for this assignment (later you may bring in the other sources or switch to another source)


Of the 3-5 potential data sources, pick 1 to focus on for this task. Build an R script or markdown file that reads in, formats, and visualizes the data using the principles of exploratory analysis.
CAUTION: You may want to store your data outside of the repository so it doesn’t try to upload to GitHub. There is a space limit on free GitHub and you cannot push large datasets there.
- Write a short summary of the read-in process and some coding secrets you learned.
- Include two to three quick visualizations that you used to check the quality of your data.
- Summarize the limitations of the compiled data in addressing your original question.
